clue.text: Cattle farm is charging fee for someone using their brand

indicators.note: to charge something is to load or fill it, so the fee is filled with the other words

parts.note: taken as written; it is the outer piece
a ranch is a farm for raising cattle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ranch is charging a fee to someone who wants to use its cattle brand.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'brand' sounds like the hot iron used on cattle; in the definition it is a trading name.
explanation.definitionFit: A franchisee pays a company for the right to trade under its brand name and system.

clue.text: Unable to move? Stop eating

definitions.meaning: second meaning: to go without food deliberately

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes the two parts look like cause and remedy; they are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means firmly fixed in place, and the verb means abstaining from food for a period.

clue.text: Hard translating Urdu so beginning with shortest word?

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so these letters are rendered in a new order
tells us one piece is placed at the very start of the other

parts.note: the indefinite article is the shortest word in English, a single letter
these six letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Translating Urdu is hard, so should one start with the shortest word?
explanation.walkthrough: The shortest word in English is the one-letter article, placed in front of the rearranged URDU SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Arduous means demanding great effort, a straightforward synonym for hard.

clue.text: Composer praised battery- powered PSV's capacity, ultimately under 100

indicators.note: in a down entry, being under something means coming after it, so the rest follows the number

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
to laud is to praise
a PSV, public service vehicle, is a bus; a battery-powered one is an e-bus
the possessive ending taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of capacity

explanation.surface: A transport review praises an electric bus for its carrying capacity.
explanation.walkthrough: PSV stands for public service vehicle, a British licensing term covering buses. The number 100 sits on top in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Debussy was a French composer known for impressionist works such as Clair de lune.

clue.text: 'Shut up,' mum snarled in fury

indicators.note: something snarled is tangled up, so these letters are knotted into a new order
signals that the tangled word is placed inside the word for anger

parts.note: ire is anger, the outer piece
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A mother, in a fury, snarls at someone to shut up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' looks like the words mum is snarling, but it is the definition, meaning to confine.
explanation.definitionFit: To immure someone is to enclose or imprison them within walls, which is shutting them up.

clue.text: Really boring celebrity turned up — Joe Bloggs?

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so one word drills into the other
in a down entry, turning a word up reads it from bottom to top

parts.note: a big name is a famous person
really and very are both intensifiers

explanation.surface: A dull celebrity shows up, an utterly ordinary person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull but means drilling into. Joe Bloggs is the British name for a hypothetical ordinary person.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyman is the typical ordinary person, just as Joe Bloggs is the British stand-in name for an average man.

clue.text: Abandon surgical procedure that doctor has started

indicators.note: the doctor's abbreviation is what the word starts with, placed first

parts.note: standard abbreviation for doctor
short for operation

explanation.surface: A patient abandons an operation that the surgeon has already begun.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop a plan or project is to give it up, the same as abandoning it.

clue.text: Safety barrier coming down with something underneath end of bar

indicators.note: in a down entry, underneath means placed below, so this piece comes second
only the final letter of the following word is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of bar
falling ill, as when coming down with a bug

explanation.surface: A safety rail, coming down, has something underneath the end of a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming down' looks like a physical fall, but 'coming down with something' means catching an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A railing is a fence of rails, used as a barrier to stop people falling.

clue.text: Seal tampered with in larder? That's funny

definitions.note: a noun here: a funny is a joke

indicators.note: something tampered with has been interfered with, so its letters are disturbed
the disturbed letters go inside the word for a storeroom

parts.note: a pantry is a food store, a larder; it is the outer piece
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone finds the seal on a food jar in the larder broken and thinks it odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' reads as the adjective 'strange', but here it is a noun, a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasantry is a light joking remark, which is what a funny is.

clue.text: Colt perhaps mixture of dam and sire

indicators.note: a mixture blends things together, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young male horse is, naturally, the product of its mother and father.
explanation.walkthrough: Dam and sire are a horse's mother and father, and a colt is a young horse, but here Colt is the gun maker.
explanation.definitionFit: A Colt revolver is an example of a sidearm, a pistol worn at the side.

clue.text: Later, darling heard through door from the bedroom

indicators.note: heard means the words are taken by their sound rather than their spelling

parts.note: later on: the French word sounds like this
sweet is a term of endearment

explanation.surface: Someone calls 'later, darling' as their partner disappears through the bedroom door.
explanation.walkthrough: The English pronunciation of the French phrase is roughly 'on sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: An en suite bathroom is attached to a bedroom and reached directly through its own door.

clue.text: Ramshackle huts do have power, a long walk from Winchester

indicators.note: ramshackle means tumbledown and disordered, so these letters fall into a new order

parts.note: these six letters rearranged
to own is to have
sway is power or influence

explanation.surface: Tumbledown huts have power, a long hike out of Winchester.
explanation.walkthrough: The South Downs are chalk hills in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The South Downs Way is a national trail of about 100 miles running from Winchester to Eastbourne.

clue.text: Duke interrupts enquiry about health that's cheeky

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the standard greeting asking after someone's wellbeing
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A duke breaks in while someone asks after his health, which is rather impudent.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is an indignant response to impertinence, just as 'that's cheeky' is.

clue.text: That thing's a little kitschy

indicators.note: a little of the next word means only a small piece of it is taken

parts.note: letters two to four

explanation.surface: Something is described as being a bit tasteless.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive pronoun means belonging to that thing, matching 'that thing's'.

clue.text: For second dissertation substitute part

parts.note: pro means in favour of
S is the abbreviation for second
a thesis is a long academic dissertation

explanation.surface: A student submits a second dissertation as a stand-in for part of the course.
explanation.definitionFit: A prosthesis is an artificial body part, such as a limb, that replaces a missing one.

clue.text: Stay permanently on edge

parts.note: re means on or concerning
a side is an edge or border

explanation.surface: Someone is told they will be living permanently on a knife edge.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there as a settled home.

clue.text: Bug perhaps gone wandering on 11D?

indicators.note: wandering means straying from a set course, so these letters stray into a new order
in an across entry, one piece being on another means it follows it

parts.note: the answer at 11 down is a long-distance footpath
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An insect has wandered off along a hiking trail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' reads as an insect on the trail, but here it means a germ.
explanation.definitionFit: A pathogen is an organism that causes disease, and a bug is the informal word for such a germ.

clue.text: Shelter outside golf club hotel after venue's evacuated

indicators.note: signals the order of the pieces, the club and hotel following on
an evacuated place is emptied of contents, so only its outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of venue
the R and A, the Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Golfers take shelter outside the clubhouse hotel once the venue has been cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: The R and A is the Scottish golf club at St Andrews that governs the game's rules.
explanation.definitionFit: A verandah is a roofed platform along the outside of a house, giving shelter.

clue.text: I wouldn't say anything walks in slaughterhouse

parts.note: the hush sound of someone keeping quiet
to amble is to walk slowly

explanation.surface: A witness won't talk about what goes on in an abattoir.
explanation.walkthrough: The first phrase sounds like a reticent witness, but it stands for the call for silence.
explanation.definitionFit: A shambles was originally a meat market or butcher's slaughterhouse; the modern sense of a mess comes from it.

clue.text: Topless baby and bottomless baby no good at all

indicators.note: without its top, which in a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written, before losing its first letter

indicators.note: without its bottom, so the last letter of the word goes

parts.note: as an adjective, baby means small, before losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A baby without a top and a baby without a bottom is a terrible state of dress.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'baby' is an adjective, as in baby carrots, meaning small.
explanation.definitionFit: Abysmal means extremely bad, so very poor that it is no good at all.

clue.text: Old cast

definitions.meaning: first meaning: previous, as in a one-time holder of a post
second meaning: a mould or frame used to shape something

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old cast' suggests a previous set of actors; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means earlier or previous; the noun is a shaping tool or mould, like a cast.

clue.text: Flipping popular vermouth, something to get hammered with?

definitions.text: Flipping popular vermouth, something to get hammered with

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it the other way, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
it is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
a ram is a device for battering or hammering

explanation.surface: A well-known vermouth brand is offered as a way to get drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the cocktail as well as building it: a Martini is popular, contains vermouth, and gets you hammered, meaning drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A martini is a cocktail of gin and vermouth, and Martini is also a famous brand of the fortified wine.

clue.text: Member that grabs leg right outside church

indicators.note: in a down entry, the right is placed beyond the church, following it

parts.note: pins is slang for legs
CE is the Church of England
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A member of the congregation grabs someone's leg just outside the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' reads as a person, but here it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pincer is the claw of a crab or lobster, a limb that grips things.

clue.text: Barge Olympian on track

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small coastal sailing vessel or barge
second meaning: Sir Chris ..., British track cycling champion

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barge' looks like a verb, an athlete shoving on the track; it is a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoy is an old type of heavy barge, and Chris Hoy won six Olympic golds in track cycling.

clue.text: Still pen and paper for the auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: writing materials, spelt with an E

explanation.surface: An accountant still asks for pen and paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant; it means a hearer. The two spellings, with E and with A, sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationary means not moving, which is what still means.

clue.text: Children realise what starts dad off

parts.note: to see is to understand or realise

indicators.note: what a word starts with is its first letter alone

parts.note: the first letter of dad

explanation.surface: Children work out what sets their father off.
explanation.definitionFit: Seed is a biblical and literary word for offspring or descendants.

clue.text: Dog does my head in always barking

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go wildly out of order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of always

explanation.surface: A constantly barking dog drives its owner mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does my head in' is British slang for annoys me; here it is split into fodder and a first-letter selector. 'Barking' also means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The Samoyed is a fluffy white Siberian breed of dog.

clue.text: Author with another sea snail holding the end of it

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so the shell goes around the letter

parts.note: a cowrie is a sea snail with a glossy shell

indicators.note: only the final letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of it

explanation.surface: A writer works with another author on a book about sea snails.
explanation.definitionFit: To co-write is to write something jointly, being its author together with another person.

clue.text: Highly paid lawyer likes dancing after taking Ecstasy

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and settle in a new order
taking something away removes it, so the drug's letter is subtracted

parts.note: taken as written
E is the street name for the drug ecstasy; it is removed

explanation.surface: A wealthy lawyer enjoys dancing after taking ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After taking Ecstasy' suggests a drug-fuelled night; here 'taking' means taking away.
explanation.definitionFit: A silk is a King's Counsel, a senior barrister who wears a silk gown and commands high fees.

clue.text: Helicopter's well built, guarantee given by Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts are exchanged

parts.note: burly means strong and heavily built
giving your word is a guarantee or promise

explanation.surface: A sturdy helicopter is promised by a man named Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of 'burly word' gives 'whirly bird'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whirlybird is informal slang for a helicopter, from its spinning rotor blades.
